lesson.title: The Uninvited Third Party on the Line
lesson.summary: A man in the middle attack occurs when an attacker secretly positions themselves between two communicating parties, able to observe or alter the traffic passing between them while each side believes it is talking directly to the other.
lesson.body:
Most network protocols are built around an assumption: that when device A sends something to device B, it actually reaches B, and that what A receives back genuinely came from B. A man in the middle, or MITM, attack breaks exactly that assumption. The attacker inserts themselves into the path between two communicating parties, often by way of a spoofing technique like the ones described in the previous chapter, and from that position can silently read the traffic passing through, alter it, or both, all while each legitimate party believes it's still communicating directly and privately with the other.

A concrete scenario makes this tangible. Imagine a user on a shared network, a coffee shop, for example, connecting to their bank's website. If an attacker on that same network manages to position themselves between the user's laptop and the router, perhaps by exploiting local network trust the way MAC spoofing does, every packet the laptop sends toward the bank passes through the attacker's machine first. Without any protection in place, the attacker could read the user's login credentials as they go by, or even alter the page content being returned. This is precisely the scenario TLS was designed to defeat: TLS doesn't just encrypt the connection, it also authenticates the server's identity through its certificate, so the user's browser can detect if it's actually talking to an attacker's machine impersonating the bank rather than the bank itself, and refuse to proceed. This is why a MITM attack against a properly configured TLS connection generally has to attack the trust chain itself, for example by trying to present a fraudulent certificate, rather than simply intercepting the traffic, since intercepted but properly authenticated and encrypted traffic is unreadable and untamperable to the attacker sitting in the middle.

This also illustrates why protocol design matters so much, echoing the broader idea of a protocol as an agreed set of rules two parties follow. A protocol that only encrypts traffic but never authenticates who is on the other end is still vulnerable to a MITM attack, because encryption alone stops eavesdropping on the wire but does nothing to confirm that the wire actually leads to the party you think it does. It's the combination, encryption plus authentication of identity, that closes the gap, and that combination is exactly what a well configured cipher suite within TLS is built to provide, tying this attack directly back to why TLS's authentication step is not optional.
